feat: ingest Capital IQ's new per-statement .xlsx exports

CIQ replaced its export interface: one .xlsx per statement instead of one .xls
workbook per company, metadata rows instead of a title row, subtotals marked by
indent rather than bold, and several line items renamed. xlrd 2.x cannot open
.xlsx at all, so ciq_source.py presents the new files as a legacy-shaped virtual
workbook and every downstream parser, column matcher and formula copier stays
as it was. Statement and period type come from file content, because CIQ's
" (1)"/" (2)" re-download suffixes do not say which export they are.

The traps in the new format were silent rather than loud:

- Key Stats items resolve by name, and six required refs (Minority Interest,
  Effective Tax Rate %, Total Cash & ST Investments, Net Rental Exp., Total
  Shares Out. on Balance Sheet Date, Curr. Port. of Leases) no longer existed
  under those names. resolve_formula mapped a missing required item to row 1,
  the header row, producing a plausible-looking wrong formula. ALIASES maps the
  renames back to the legacy spelling, and unresolved_items() now leaves the row
  blank and reports it.
- Effective Tax Rate and Payout Ratio now arrive in percentage points instead of
  fractions; unscaled, (1 - tax rate) turned ROIC into -1348% instead of 42%.
- extract_code_from_filename picked the export year ('2026') out of the new
  filenames as the stock code, and batch mode would have routed each statement
  file as its own company.

Found while validating 分众传媒 (002027) into 传媒, fixed here as well: 扣非 LTM
summed the last four quarter columns including a not-yet-reported one; Net

净利息收益率 at #DIV/0!; and quarter columns received ROE formulas that can never
resolve, since CIQ exports no quarterly balance sheet - existing tabs leave that

feat(env): the decode boundary, and the workbook behind EvalEnv

M4b1 of the tier-D1 ladder: `pkg/workbook.zig` gains the `EvalEnv`
adapter, and `src/formula/` gains the two files it reads a package
through — the XML decode boundary and the decoded symbol layer.

Decoding is split by CARRIER CLASS, which is the row's hardest claim
and the one that fails silently when it is wrong. FORMULA carriers
(`<f>` bodies, defined-name bodies, table formulas) get XML entity
decoding ONLY: a literal `_x0041_` written inside a formula is still
`_x0041_` when the tokenizer sees it. STRING carriers (shared, inline,
`t="str"`, and the ST_Xstring-typed identifiers) get entities THEN
ST_Xstring, with rich runs concatenated in document order and `<rPh>`
phonetics excluded. Authoring inverts the same split, and because a
formula has no second escape layer, a formula carrying a character XML
cannot represent refuses instead of inventing one.

The corpus decided four rows against the plan. `wdi_excel.xlsx` omits
`r` on `<row>` as well as `<c>` — 13.9M cells whose coordinates exist
only as a rule — and `src/xlsx.zig` already reconstructs it, so
refusing r-less rows would have refused a workbook this repo reads.
`poi_poc_shared_strings.xlsx` carries `<row r="0">`, which the typed
reader silently skips and this boundary refuses: a dropped row
recalculates as blank cells. §9's `max_modeled_cells` (64M) turns out
not to bound memory at all — that workbook models at ~7 GB — so the
number stands as specified and the gap is recorded for M5's byte
budget. And the shared-string run limit had to become per string
rather than per part.

The namespace preflight sweeps every part the run will read before any
of them is decoded: a scanner that literal-matches `<sheetData>` reads
an unknown vocabulary as an empty sheet, and recalculating an empty
sheet writes zeroes over real data.

Two build-graph consequences. The engine is now ONE module: reaching
`env`, `value` and `decode` separately would compile `env.zig` twice
and build an `EvalEnv` the evaluator could not accept, and
`src/xlsx.zig`'s relative import of the rewriter would have put
`tokenizer.zig` in two modules at once. The pkg-facing module
deliberately declares no `zlsx_casefold`, which is test-only and would
claim `src/unicode/casefold.zig` for two modules.

Also fixes a latent double-free found by this row's allocation-failure
sweep: `Workbook.open` and `Workbook.empty` kept an armed `errdefer`
over a `PartStore` that `fromStore` already frees on failure, so a
workbook with no `xl/workbook.xml` segfaulted instead of returning
`MissingWorkbookPart`.

The adapter is proven by the fake's own suite — one test body, two
harnesses, and the adapter's harness authors real sheet XML and reads
it back through the boundary rather than injecting cells.

3152 -> 3560 tests, `zig build` and `zig build fuzz` green.

Teach the workbook the curve, and make a missing driver fail loudly

Three problems, one of which the equivalence test found the moment it was
given the chance.

The driver-sheet writer only emits numeric properties, so the nested growth
curve was skipped entirely. The formulas would then have had no cell to point
at — and `d()` answered a missing driver with the string "0", which means the
workbook would have shown flat growth while the engine compounded. A
spreadsheet that looks perfect and disagrees with the plan exported beside it is
the single most damaging thing this product could ship, so `d()` now throws, and
`dOpt` exists for the drivers whose absence is a shape rather than a bug.

`curveAt` emits `projectCurve` as a live Excel expression, branch for branch.
That is why the growth module uses POWER and never EXP or LN: the evaluator in
tests/helpers/xlsx-eval.ts has no EXP, and more importantly the TypeScript and
the spreadsheet have to be the same expression or the workbook stops being the
model.

And the test earned its place immediately. The new fixture — a plan whose stream
carries a saturating curve — failed on month two: the workbook said 5,466.24
where the engine said 5,551.82. The subscription formula was still multiplying
by the legacy growth rate, because one of my edits had silently not matched.
Every other stream had been converted; that one had not, and nothing else in the
suite would have noticed. exceljs writes formulas and never evaluates them, so a
wrong formula ships looking perfect.

Keep quoted values text when reading visigrid-json

Step 2 of the text-typed cells spec, and it needed no format change: the
distinction was already on the wire. FullCell.value is a serde_json::Value,
so "007" is a JSON string and 7.0 a JSON number, and the writer emits both
faithfully. The reader matched on the type, flattened it to a string, and
handed it to set_value — which inferred the type over again. Recognised,
then discarded one line later, under a comment reading "typed value".

That is why step 1 delivered nothing in the server. The xlsx reader kept
007 through import and the first recalc turned it back into 7, because
every server-side recalc runs json-full through this path. Verified: the
import-then-recalc diff was three values collapsing and is now empty.

Quoted means text, decided on the failure direction rather than on which
is more often intended. Today's behaviour destroys data silently; a
foreign document that quoted a number now shows text, which is visible
and fixable. Our own writers only quote what was text, so round trips are
exact either way, and the importer says how many quoted values read as
numbers so the ambiguity is discoverable rather than deduced from a total
that came out wrong.

Formulas still coerce: LEN("007") is 1 and ISNUMBER is TRUE, because a
cell reference is read through CellLookup::get_text and re-typed from the
string (eval.rs:540). get_cell_value is a default method built on the
same call, so the loss is at the trait's foundation. That is step 3 and
it is now the visible seam — the cell stores and displays 007 while
formulas see 7.

Recompute the workbook's analytics outside the spreadsheet

The Validation tab reports 23 of 23 checks passing under a green banner.
Both numbers are produced by the same workbook whose formulas are the
thing in question, so neither carries independent weight: a wrong
formula reports a pass exactly as confidently as a right one.

validate_portfolio.py reads only inputs, per-holding cost and market
value, the sector table, the risk-free rate, the market return and beta,
and recomputes 27 derived figures in Python. It never reads a cell
holding a tick or a pass count. Three groups: portfolio accounting
including every holding's gain, return and weight; concentration
including the Herfindahl-Hirschman index and effective positions; and
the CAPM and risk ratios, each rebuilt from its own definition. All 27
reconcile on this workbook.

The script is itself tested, because one that has only seen a correct
workbook proves nothing. Eleven tests copy the workbook, change one
cached cell and assert that specific figure is reported wrong: a broken
total, a single corrupted holding weight, a wrong index, a broken CAPM
return, a broken Sharpe ratio and a cell holding a division by zero.

Two things worth recording for anyone extending this:

- openpyxl holds either formulas or cached results, never both, so
  saving a workbook with it discards every cached value and the
  validator then reads nothing. tests/xlsx_surgery.py edits the cached
  value directly in the sheet XML instead, leaving the formula, the
  styles and every other cell untouched.
- Effective positions is the reciprocal of the HOLDING-level index, not
  the sector-level one shown in the HHI Index row. Checking it against
  the wrong basis reported a defect that did not exist, so a test now
  pins the right one.

CI runs the tests first and the real workbook second. Running only the
second would show a green tick even if every comparison were inverted.

Add an Excel model of the momentum calculation

node --use-system-ca momentum-model.js CRWD writes a three-sheet workbook —
Bars, Factors, Score — in which every cell is a live formula over the daily
bars. It is not a picture of the calculation: change a close price and the score
moves, because the workbook does the arithmetic itself.

Bars carries the sessions newest-first, as the app holds them, plus the running
intermediates the factors need — log returns, both moving averages, and RSI.
Wilder smoothing is a recursive column seeded with a simple fourteen-day average
at the old end and smoothed upward, because Wilder runs oldest-first while the
sheet reads newest-first.

Factors shows each raw measurement as a formula reading Bars, then the curve
that turns it into a sub-score, with the centre and scale beside it so the fixed
scale is visible rather than buried. Score renormalises the weights, produces
the 0-100 and the 1-10, and then subtracts what the app reported when the file
was written. That check is the point: on CRWD it reads 72.1 against 72.1, with
every factor agreeing within the two decimals the stored breakdown rounds to.

Written by hand because an xlsx is a zip of XML and a spreadsheet library would
be a fourth dependency for a one-off explainer — the same reasoning that sends
mail over plain fetch. Excel is told to recalculate on load, since no cached
values are stored.

One bug worth recording: values[k] in the app is bar k back from today, which
lands on sheet row D+1+k. Writing D+k reads the session next door, and every
return in the model is a difference between two of these — it produced four
wrong formulas before the check against the app caught it. There is a B(k)
helper now so the offset is written once.

The output is gitignored. It goes stale the moment prices move, and regenerating
it takes a second.

Rebuild the Excel dashboard as a formula-driven workbook

Reworks datamind/dashboard.py to match the architecture of a hand-built
interactive Excel dashboard (per a reference financial dashboard file)
instead of writing static computed numbers into cells:

- Dashboard sheet: up to 4 dropdown filters (data-validated against a
  hidden Lists sheet), 4 KPI cards, and up to 5 charts - a trend line,
  a doughnut for share-of-total, plain bars, and red/teal diverging
  bars for any metric whose per-category values can go negative
  (decided from the real computed data, never guessed).
- Calc sheet: the formula engine. Dropdowns resolve to SUMIFS/
  AVERAGEIFS/COUNTIFS wildcard filters ("All" -> "*"); every KPI card
  and chart is a live formula against Data, so changing a filter
  recalculates the whole dashboard - matching the reference file's
  "no hardcoded numbers" approach. Median/distinct-count KPIs (no
  *IFS equivalent in Excel) fall back to a one-time computed value.
- KPI Reference sheet: definitions/formula/why-it-matters/good-bad
  result/best-visualization table, plus insights/risks/opportunities/
  recommendations (previously on a separate Overview sheet).
- Data sheet gains a derived "<col> (Month)" helper column for any
  date field used in a trend chart, so SUMIFS can group by month.

Since this environment's LibreOffice install can't actually open/
recalculate xlsx files (verified: even a plain .txt conversion fails),
added an independent SUMIFS/AVERAGEIFS/COUNTIFS formula interpreter in
the test suite that parses the generated formula strings and
re-evaluates them against the dataframe, to catch a plausible-looking
but wrong formula (bad column letter, off-by-one row range) that
static inspection alone would miss.

Expands the Gemini plan schema (agent.py) with filter_columns and
richer per-KPI reference fields, and fixes a latent bug where the
dashboard-plan prompt's JSON schema example used doubled {{ }} braces
that were never templated, so Gemini was literally being shown
invalid/confusing JSON syntax in the instructions.

db: run the cascade on a graph nobody typed — the spreadsheet test

Six days established the shape and the killer. The instrument catches system
errors rather than fraud, and both catches rest on one condition: somebody had
to write the citation down. That is daily work for a benefit that arrives only
when something goes wrong — the shape of every ledger nobody fills in.

So the test was not a better store but whether the condition can be removed by
going where the dependency graph already exists. It can, for the expensive
half. A workbook is generated and read back with zipfile and ElementTree
alone — no library, no server, no permission — and the cascade runs on it:

  line_b (B2) turns out wrong -> subtotal, vat, total, margin, over_ceiling

Five links, and the number of links anybody typed is ZERO. Ranges are expanded,
so SUM(B1:B4) resolves to the four cells it names nowhere.

The generated workbook is a real .xlsx and not a private dialect: LibreOffice
opens it and recomputes every formula (subtotal 7250, total 8700, margin 3700).

What the human still owes, measured rather than hoped: the graph is free, the
GROUNDS are not. A sheet knows the total is subtotal plus VAT; it has no idea
B1 came from invoice 17. But annotation is owed only on the LEAVES — every
derived figure inherits by computation. On this sheet that is 54%, and the
sheet is small; the honest number is the measured one, not the flattering one
a formula-heavy model would give.

Named rather than skipped: cross-sheet and cross-file references are not
followed; a pasted value is indistinguishable from a typed one, so the London
Whale's copy-paste stays invisible exactly as it was in the model; and a wrong
formula remains an honest dependency.

feat(rubric): custom equations, guided builder, calculated columns, live-formula .xlsx export, in-app controls

Adds user-defined equations at every stage of scoring, a guided way to
build them, formula-driven columns, and a native workbook export, and
replaces the browser-native controls with app-styled ones. Still a
single index.html with no dependencies and no code comments.

Custom equations
- Add EXPR, a small expression engine (tokenizer, precedence-climbing
  parser, evaluator) with no eval() or new Function(). Supports
  + - * / % ^ (right-associative), comparisons, && || !, the ternary
  operator and a whitelisted set of functions (abs, sqrt, exp, ln,
  log10, log2, pow, min, max, floor, ceil, round, sign, tanh, sin, cos,
  atan, clamp, if). Unknown names, unknown functions and syntax errors
  are reported before anything runs.
- Add a "Custom equation" value function: x is the raw value; min, max,
  mean, median, std, n, sum, pi and e are available, plus named
  constants. Output is clamped to 0-1 and flagged when out of range.
  Direction is encoded in the equation, so the toggle is hidden for it.
- Equation editor on criteria cards: live validation, a sample
  evaluation, insert chips, a constants field, a "Write your own
  equation" shortcut and a "Start from a template" menu (7 curves).
- Add a "Scoring method" panel on the Rank tab: weighted sum, geometric
  mean, harmonic mean, TOPSIS, or a custom combining equation using
  per-criterion scores, w_<id> weight shares, wsum, wgeo, whm, wmin,
  wmax, wpow(p), n and constants, with 4 blend templates.
- Treat custom value functions that reference column statistics as
  relative scoring so the Relative badge, rank-reversal check and
  assumptions note stay accurate.
- Centralise the direction rule in dirApplies().

Guided equation builder
- "Build step by step" on criteria cards: pick a shape (straight line,
  fast then flat, slow then fast, S-curve, pass/fail at a limit, peak
  at a target), a direction and a few labelled values seeded from the
  data, with a live preview. Invalid input is blocked. Writes a normal
  custom equation that stays editable.

Calculated columns
- A criterion can carry a formula over other criteria (e.g. cost /
  seats), evaluated before scoring in dependency order; cycles resolve
  to missing values. Columns are read-only in Data (marked with a
  function glyph) and feed scoring, flip thresholds, robustness and
  Monte Carlo; they are skipped in the per-input tolerance list.

Workbook export
- Add "Download workbook (.xlsx)": a dependency-free writer (stored
  zip with CRC-32, hand-built SpreadsheetML) producing a Data sheet and
  a Scores sheet with live formulas: normalizers over live column
  ranges, calculated columns as formulas, totals for weighted sum,
  geometric/power mean and custom equations, percentile and categorical
  criteria, missing-value policies, hard gates and incomplete-data
  exclusions as live Status formulas, rank over passing options,
  soft-gate penalties, and the app's own total for comparison.
- Percentile scores use COUNTIF instead of RANK.AVG, which needs a
  special prefix in .xlsx and showed #NAME? in some spreadsheet apps.
- Verified by recalculating 36 exports (4 examples x 9 scoring
  methods) in LibreOffice against the app's totals: no mismatches.
- Not modelled: the "redistribute" missing policy; TOPSIS is exported
  as static totals.
- Remove the legacy .csv spreadsheet export, which could produce wrong
  formulas, in favour of the workbook.

App-styled controls
- Replace every native <select> with a custom listbox dropdown with
  full keyboard support; it opens upward near the window bottom and
  closes on outside click, scroll and resize.
- Replace native number inputs with in-app fields with +/- steppers and
  arrow-key stepping; invalid typed weights are ignored.
- Restyle range sliders; replace title tooltips with in-app tooltips;

- Add shared field, textarea and chip styles and the missing .linkbtn

Fixes

feat(import): accept Excel workbooks, and spreadsheets dropped on the scanner (#148)

A cellar spreadsheet had no working door. The scan screen accepted only
image/* and application/pdf, so a .csv or .xlsx dropped there was refused
with no explanation and no redirect; /import accepted .csv but rejected
Excel outright with "Only .csv files are accepted."

Excel is now converted to CSV before it touches anything else, so the
entire existing pipeline runs on it unchanged — header matching, row
validation, dedup keys, LWIN matching, chunk planning, digests, revert.
The conversion is the only spreadsheet-aware code in the import domain;
everything after it sees bytes indistinguishable from an uploaded .csv,
rather than a second ingestion path that could drift from the first.

The reader runs server-side (POST /api/import/convert) because exceljs is
far too heavy to ship to the browser — the build confirms zero client
chunks reference it. The client calls it the moment a workbook is chosen
and swaps in the returned CSV, so a large sheet is split into chunks by
exactly the same client-side splitter a large .csv is. Converting on the
server while the browser keeps the CSV text is what preserves chunking;
converting in the browser would have cost ~1MB of bundle, and converting
without handing the text back would have broken every file over MAX_ROWS.

A spreadsheet dropped on the scan screen is now parked and the operator is
taken to /import, which picks it up and behaves as if they had chosen it
there. The handoff is single-consumption so a later visit cannot re-import
a file already dealt with, and React's development double-invoke cannot
import it twice.

Details worth knowing:
- Only the first worksheet is read, and the UI says which sheet it used
  and how many it saw. A silent one-of-four import is invisible until the
  totals come out wrong.
- Formula cells contribute their cached result, never the formula text.
- Rows are padded to a rectangle. exceljs drops trailing empty cells, so a
  sheet with an empty last column produced short rows whose values then
  shifted into the wrong columns downstream. Caught by its own test.
- .xls is refused by name with a message saying to re-save as .xlsx, since
  exceljs cannot read the legacy binary format at all.
- MAX_SPREADSHEET_ROWS / MAX_SPREADSHEET_CSV_BYTES bound how far a small
  ZIP-compressed upload may expand; exceeding either is a 413, not a 422.
- exceljs pulls a vulnerable uuid, so uuid is pinned via the existing
  override mechanism. pnpm audit is back to the single unfixable
  extract-zip advisory. exceljs only calls uuid.v4 when WRITING conditional
  formatting, a path this code never takes, and it reads workbooks fine on
  the pinned version.

Spreadsheet printing: what goes on a page, and how wide a column is

Looking at a National Tax Agency liquor-tax workbook: five sheets that Excel
prints on seven pages come out of ours on twenty-two. Three things were wrong,
none of them the whole story.

**Cells with nothing in them were being printed.** The print range came from
`extent`, which is every cell present in the map — and xlsx files carry cells
that hold only a style, no value, no border, no fill. That workbook declares
twelve columns on its first sheet where nine hold anything, and eighty rows on
its last where seventy-one do. `print_extent` stops at the last cell worth
printing, and keeps empty cells that carry a border or a fill, because those
are part of the ruled form.

**Column width was a linear guess.** Excel's rule is `trunc(width × MDW) + 5`
in pixels, the five being the cell's inner padding and its gridline; ours was
`width × 2.0mm`. At the default width of 8.43 the two agree to within a tenth
of a millimetre, so this changes no page count here — but they diverge in both
directions, and a form of narrow columns adds up the padding the old formula
never charged for.

**Rows with no stated height fell to a fixed 7mm** rather than the sheet's own
`defaultRowHeight`. Almost every row in this workbook states its height, so
again no page count moved, but a sheet that leaves its rows alone was being
laid out half again too tall.

Together these take it from twenty-two pages to twenty-one. That is the honest
number.

I should record how I nearly claimed more. Comparing our widths against a
formula I wrote from memory, every sheet looked 8% too wide, and correcting to
that wrong formula took the count to fourteen — a satisfying result from
columns that were simply too narrow. The test I wrote afterwards, checking the
default width against its known 64 pixels, is what caught it. The formula in
this commit is the real one and the count went back to twenty-one.

So the three-fold page count is still unexplained. What I can say from
measurement: the reference PDF lays about 182mm of ink across each page, and
our own arithmetic makes the widest sheet 388mm against Excel's implied 364mm.
Six per cent, somewhere in the column widths or in a couple of columns that
still should not be printing. Finding it means measuring against the rendered
reference rather than against a formula.

Two tests, each confirmed to fail when its fix is reverted: the print range
stops at the last cell with a value or a border while a style-only cell does
not extend it, and a column of the default width comes out at Excel's 64
pixels.

Core tests pass with no locale, calc/writer/ui with OFFICE_LANG=ja, the page
image regression is unchanged, and the Python scripts pass.

feat(formula): recalculate the stale formulas, and on every save (#1014)

* feat(formula): recalculate the stale formulas, and on every save

`Document::recalculate` computes the stale formula cells of an ods and an
xlsx and writes each result into the document (decision 32). It returns
the cells whose result changed, the cells of a cycle, and the cells
nothing here computes. A save recalculates first where an edit left a
formula stale (decision 33).

- A cell is stale where an edit since the last recalculation reaches it,
  where it caches no result, or where it reads what no position names: a
  name, a volatile function, a reference over several sheets. A
  structural edit makes every formula stale. `internal::Document` notes
  the edits.
- A stale cell is computed on demand, and every other cell reads as the
  file caches it. The stale cells are computed in reading order, so a
  chain down a column is one step deep at a time. A cell its own
  computation reaches is a cycle, and none of a cycle gets a result.
- `SheetAdapter::sheet_set_result` writes a result and keeps the formula.
  An ods takes the type the cell's data style shows: a date, a time or a
  number. It states an error with `calcext:value-type`, and declares the
  namespace where an older file does not. An xlsx writes `v` and `t`.
- A cell the evaluator has no answer for stays as before: an ods states
  no result, and an xlsx keeps the one it had and asks a reader to compute
  it on load.
- `sheet_visit_formulas` now states the size of a repeat, so a stale
  formula a repeat stands for has no answer, rather than its other
  positions reading the stale result.

* fix(formula): give an array formula no result, and bound the depth of a recalculation

- Decision 29 gives an array formula no answer, but recalculate computed
  one as a plain formula and wrote the result: an xlsx
  {=SUM(A1:A2*B1:B2)} got A1*B1 after an edit. The formula visitor now
  states an array formula and the range it fills, and a recalculation
  treats that range as it treats a repeat. A formula that reads a cell of
  the range is stale with it, and gets no result.
- The ods parser skipped table:covered-table-cell and relied on a span to
  account for it. An array formula's range has no span, so every cell
  after one of its covered cells read a column to the left.
- A level of the recalculation takes about a kilobyte of stack, so 1024
  levels could overflow a mobile thread. The depth limit is now 64. A read
  that reaches it computes the far end of the chain first and then tries
  again, so a chain up a column of 1100 cells still gets every result. A
  depth-limited result was cached as no answer before, which left the
  whole chain above it without one.
- SheetCellSource::sheets is back, as the recalculation reads it.

feat(formula): the functions of mathematics and aggregation (#1009)

* feat(formula): the functions of mathematics and aggregation

The evaluator knows 48 functions of mathematics and aggregation: `SUM`,
`AVERAGE`, `COUNT`, `ROUND`, `MOD`, `SUMPRODUCT`, the trigonometric
functions and others. LibreOffice gave the result of each case in the
tests, and Excel's documentation the result of the Excel dialect.

- An aggregate reads the numbers of a range. LibreOffice reads a boolean
  cell as 1, and Excel skips it. A text stated as an argument reads as a
  number in Excel. LibreOffice refuses one, function by function, so it
  gives no answer.
- LibreOffice adds left to right and makes a sum that cancels 0. A sum
  that nearly cancels has no answer in Excel.
- A rounding reads the number to 15 significant digits first, so
  `ROUND(2.675;2)` is 2.68. Where reading it to 12 digits rounds it
  elsewhere, the number is too close to the edge, and it has no answer.
- An argument outside a function's domain is `#NUM!` in Excel. LibreOffice
  states a code of its own (`Err:502`), which a file cannot hold as an
  error, so it has no answer.
- `SUMPRODUCT` reads its arguments in an array context: an operator reads
  every cell of a range. A function inside that context has no answer yet.

The corpus test now answers 9674 of 15160 formulas, and all of them match.

* fix(formula): add an ods sum as LibreOffice's KahanSum does

LibreOffice adds SUM, AVERAGE, SUMSQ and SUMPRODUCT with KahanSum, a
Neumaier sum that holds back the last number. Adding left to right with
approxAdd gave 0.5 for SUM(1;1E20;-1E20;0.5), where LibreOffice gives 1.5.
VAR takes its mean with KahanSum and each deviation with approxSub.

Also:
- An ods MOD whose remainder precision put outside the divisor is #VALUE!,
  as ScMod decides.
- Excel documents no reading to 15 digits outside a rounding, so INT,
  MOD, QUOTIENT, EVEN, ODD and FACT give no answer in an xlsx where the
  reading changes the result. An xlsx MOD that nearly cancels has none
  either.
- COUNTBLANK of several areas has no answer.
- One nearly_cancels test holds Excel's threshold for an operator and SUM.
- The function tables are std::array.

* refactor(formula): read the numbers of an aggregate without a sentinel or a vector

collect takes the count of arguments it reads, so kth no longer passes a
last index of -1. kahan_sum and sum_of read a std::span.

feat(formula): the functions of lookup and the conditional aggregates (#1011)

* feat(formula): the functions of lookup and the conditional aggregates

The evaluator knows 14 more functions: `VLOOKUP`, `HLOOKUP`, `MATCH`,
`INDEX`, `ROW`, `COLUMN`, `ROWS`, `COLUMNS`, `COUNTIF`, `COUNTIFS`,
`SUMIF`, `SUMIFS`, `AVERAGEIF` and `AVERAGEIFS`. LibreOffice gave the
result of each case in the tests.

- A criterion and a lookup match a text without case, whatever the
  settings of the document. Only the operators follow
  `table:case-sensitive`.
- A criterion that spells a number (`"5"`, `">4"`) matches the number.
  For `=` and `<>` it also matches a text spelling it. A number criterion
  (`5`) matches no text.
- `""` matches an empty cell and an empty text, `"="` an empty cell, and
  `"<>"` every cell that is not empty.
- A wildcard, and a regular expression where the document turns them on,
  have no answer. So does an ordering of texts that holds more than
  letters and digits, as the collator of each application decides.
- An approximate lookup has an answer only for numbers in ascending
  order without a repeat at the match. Elsewhere the binary search of
  each application decides.
- `ROWS` of a whole column has no answer, as the two grids differ in
  height. A `Area` now states whether it is a whole column or row.

The corpus test now answers 14963 of 15160 formulas, and all of them
match.

* fix(formula): add an ods conditional sum as LibreOffice's KahanSum does

LibreOffice adds SUMIF, SUMIFS, AVERAGEIF and AVERAGEIFS with KahanSum
(IterateParametersIf, ParamIfsResult), as it adds SUM. The matched numbers
now go through sum_of, so an xlsx sum that nearly cancels has no answer,
as for SUM.

Also:
- Remove the copy of is_libreoffice that #1010 made shared.
- Rename the new Call::cell(position) to cell_value, apart from
  Call::cell(), the position of the formula.
- COUNTIF and COUNTIFS share one function, and so do the sum and the
  average of the matched cells.
- The tables are std::array, and the comment of cell_limit says what it
  limits.
